title: Checkpoint: Genres and Why They Work
objective: After this level you can explain why genres work and how filmmakers keep familiar formulas fresh.
summary: Genres can be defined by setting, by story shape or by style: noir may be a style, not a genre. The chapter showed genres as promises, kept fresh by new ideas, suspense and bending the rules.

cards.headline: Is film noir even a genre? Critics still argue.
cards.body: This chapter treated genres as promises. So where does one genre stop and the next begin? Britannica defines film noir as a style of filmmaking, and critics still argue over whether it is a genre at all. That argument turns out to be a neat way to sum up the chapter.

cards.headline: A place, a shape or a look
cards.body: Most genres are defined by subject or setting: the Western, the gangster film, science fiction. The musical is looser. It often has a show-business setting, but it can be about almost any subject. Film noir is looser still: the label fits mostly crime dramas, yet some critics apply it to certain Westerns and comedies, and there's a running debate over whether it's a genre at all or a style shared by many.

events.label: The Great Train Robbery sets the Western's pattern
It Happened One Night wins all five major Oscars
The Maltese Falcon adapts Hammett's hard-boiled novel
Cat People never shows its monster
Them! grows giant ants from atomic bomb tests
Mel Brooks spoofs the Western and Frankenstein

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: A genre promises something familiar and something new, and studios loved the routine it allowed. Musicals sang what speech couldn't carry. Screwball couples fought their way to love, since sparring stood in for what the code banned. Horror aimed for just-right fear. Noir and science fiction carried the worries of their time. Hitchcock showed that letting the audience in on a secret builds suspense. And once the rules were familiar, filmmakers could bend them.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Why a genre promises the familiar and the new, and why studios loved that routine.
How Westerns, musicals, screwball comedy and horror each deliver the feeling their fans expect.
Why film noir and 1950s science fiction carried the fears of their own time.
How suspense, parody and revision all play on what the audience already knows.

questions.prompt: Why is film noir so hard to call a genre?

options.label: It was only ever made by French directors
options.rationale: French critics named it, but the films were American.

options.label: It has no recognizable visual style
options.rationale: Its high-contrast look is its best-known feature.

options.label: Many see it as a style that crosses genres
Every noir is also a musical
options.rationale: Noir's label fits mostly crime dramas.

questions.explanation: Britannica defines noir as a style of filmmaking, critics argue over whether it is a genre at all, and some apply it to certain Westerns and comedies.

questions.prompt: What two things does a genre promise its audience at once?

options.label: A famous star and a guaranteed happy ending
options.rationale: Neither is part of the genre promise.

options.label: Low prices and short films
options.rationale: The promise is about the experience.

options.label: Pure repetition of the last hit
options.rationale: Pure repetition would leave out the new.

questions.explanation: A genre promises something similar to what audiences enjoyed before, and yet something quite new and different.

questions.prompt: Why can't the musical be defined by its setting the way the Western can?

options.label: Musicals are always set on a real frontier
Musicals have no plot at all
options.rationale: A musical's plot integrates musical numbers.

options.label: Musicals are defined by their lighting
A musical can be about almost any subject

questions.explanation: Most genres are defined by subject or setting, but the musical can be about almost any subject; what marks it is a plot that integrates musical numbers.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones of film genres in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: The Great Train Robbery came in 1903, It Happened One Night in 1934, The Maltese Falcon in 1941, Cat People in 1942, Them! in 1954 and Mel Brooks's spoofs in 1974.

questions.prompt: Film noir and 1950s science fiction look nothing alike, but both carry the same worry of the time: _____.

options.label: the move from silent to sound
options.rationale: Neither genre is tied to that; the move to sound came in the late 1920s.

options.label: fear of giant insects
options.rationale: Only Them! has those, and they stand for something bigger.

options.label: the decline of the Western
options.rationale: The Western was still thriving in the 1950s.

questions.explanation: Britannica links noir to the looming threat of atomic warfare, and Them!'s giant ants were mutated by atomic bomb tests.
